disease.disease_type.sql_expression: CASE WHEN instr(disease_type, '||') > 0 THEN trim(substr(disease_type, 1, instr(disease_type, '||') - 1)) ELSE trim(disease_type) END
disease.disease_type.mapping_rule: Keep only the first item of the '||'-separated list (the text before the first '||', trimmed). Values without '||' are returned unchanged (trimmed).
disease.disease_type.reason: The query groups by disease_type and filters out '' as if each disease has one type, so the column must hold a single category. The stored values are multi-valued lists, so grouping by the full string creates many one-off groups. Taking the first listed type gives one category per row, and the expression is deterministic. The first-item rule is an assumption about which type the author would treat as primary.

disease.prognosis.reason: The query uses LIKE with leading and trailing % wildcards, so it matches a term anywhere in the string. The '||'-delimited lists therefore work as stored: '%chronic%' matches every value containing 'chronic_condition', and '%high_mortality%' matches every value containing 'high_mortality'. The underscore in the LIKE pattern is a single-character wildcard, but the only stored text it could match in this data is the intended 'high_mortality' token, so no transformation is needed.

disease.disease_type.reason: The query uses case-insensitive substring LIKE tests on each category name, so the '||'-delimited lists already work: a row matches every category it contains, which is the per-category counting the author intends. No stored value needs reshaping. The non-standard token 'infectious_viral' still matches '%infectious%', so it is counted correctly without any change.

disease.treatments.mapping_rule: Rewrite each `||`-separated item into a query category, then join the categories with `||`. Items that are drug treatments (oral_medication, injection, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, biological_therapy, hormone_therapy, drug_therapy, inhaler, vaccination) become `medication`. Invasive procedures (surgery, device_implantation, radiotherapy, stem cell transplantation) become `procedure`. lifestyle_modification becomes `lifestyle`. Other items (dietary_intervention, physical_therapy, psychotherapy, regular_exercise, relaxation_techniques, meditation, laboratory_test, others, other) are left as they are or dropped, since the query does not test for them. Remove duplicate categories. A row with no mapped category keeps an empty string, which the WHERE filter then excludes.
disease.treatments.reason: The query tests treatments with LIKE for 'medication', 'procedure' and 'lifestyle'. The stored values use item names such as surgery and device_implantation, and the word 'procedure' never appears in any stored value. Only 'lifestyle' and 'medication' (inside oral_medication) match by substring today. The author's intent is a count of diseases by treatment category, which requires a judgment mapping from each item to the category name the query expects, not a positional or string-slicing expression.

disease.prognosis.reason: The query only tests whether the text contains 'chronic' (LIKE '%chronic%'). Every stored value is a '||'-joined list of controlled terms, and 'chronic' appears only inside 'chronic_condition', so the substring test correctly flags any disease whose prognosis list includes chronic_condition. No other stored term contains 'chronic', so no transformation is needed.

disease.treatments.reason: The query tests each treatment with a substring LIKE match on names that already appear verbatim in the stored values (e.g. 'injection', 'surgery', 'lifestyle_modification', 'dietary_intervention', 'physical_therapy'). Each one occurs as a whole token inside the '||'-joined lists, and none of the queried names is a substring of a different treatment. The underscore wildcard in LIKE still matches a literal underscore, so the matches are correct. Counting rows that contain each term therefore gives what the author intends without any change.

disease.disease_name.sql_expression: TRIM(CASE WHEN instr(disease_name, '||') > 0 THEN substr(disease_name, 1, instr(disease_name, '||') - 1) ELSE disease_name END)
disease.disease_name.reason: Several disease_name values are '||'-joined lists of synonyms, with the official name first. The query joins on exact equality with drug.disease_name and groups by the disease name, so each row needs its official (first-listed) name. Taking the text before the first '||' and trimming whitespace yields that name. Values without '||' are unchanged, and the first items match the drug-side names (e.g., 'Asthma', 'Hypertension', 'Depression').

drug.disease_name.mapping_rule: For each distinct stored value, take the first item of the '||'-separated list (the main disease the drug is intended to treat). Then, if that name refers to the same condition as a value in disease.disease_name, replace it with that partner-table spelling (e.g., 'Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder' -> 'Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder', 'Type 2 Diabetes' or 'Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus' -> 'Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus', 'Irritable Bowel Syndrome with Constipation' -> 'Irritable Bowel Syndrome', 'HIV infection' -> 'HIV-1 Infection', 'Gastroesophageal reflux disease' -> 'Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease', 'Benign Prostatic Hypertrophy' -> 'Benign Prostatic Hypertrophy (BPH)'). If no matching partner name exists, keep the first item as written.
drug.disease_name.reason: The query joins on exact equality of disease_name, so each drug row needs one standard disease name that appears in the disease table. Many stored values are multi-disease lists, and the first item alone still differs in spelling or wording from the partner table's names, so a simple SQL extraction would not produce matches. A per-value mapping that picks the primary indication and normalizes it to the partner spelling is needed.

drug.prescription_status.mapping_rule: Take the first item of the '||'-separated list in prescription_status, trimmed of whitespace. Single values pass through unchanged.

drug.disease_name.reason: The query uses LIKE with wildcards on both sides, so it matches a disease term anywhere in the string. Each target term (panic, ulcer, gout, diabetes, heart failure) appears in the stored values as intended, and SQLite's case-insensitive LIKE handles the capitalisation variants. drug.single_dose.mapping_rule: Map each distinct stored value to one numeric mg figure: the first dose amount in mg in the value (the first listed population's dose, e.g. 'adults 10 mg || adults 25 mg' -> 10; 'oral 400mg||oral 800mg' -> 400; 'adults 25 milligrams' -> 25; 'adults 250-500mg||children 15mg/kg daily' -> 250, the lower bound of a range). Values with no mg dose, such as 'two capsules', 'adults 2 capsules', 'adults (12 years and over) 15 mL', 'infants 40 mg per 1 mL', or 'adults and children 1 year and older [dose not specified]', map to NULL, and so do values whose only figures are in mcg, mg/kg, or mg/lb, unless the mg figure is clearly stated. Values in other units can be handled by the same rule, but any mapping that would give a number not stated as mg should be NULL.
drug.single_dose.reason: The query casts single_dose to REAL and compares it numerically, but the stored values are free text with population labels, multiple doses, ranges, and mixed units (mg, mcg, mL, capsules, mg/kg). CAST would return 0 or a wrong number for almost every row. SQLite has no regex to extract the first number reliably across these forms, so a per-value judgment mapping to the first mg dose is the accurate way to make the numeric comparison mean what the author intends.

drug.single_dose.sql_expression: CASE WHEN instr(single_dose, '||') > 0 THEN trim(substr(single_dose, 1, instr(single_dose, '||') - 1)) ELSE trim(single_dose) END
drug.single_dose.mapping_rule: Keep the first 'A || B' item of each list, trimmed of surrounding spaces; values without '||' are returned unchanged (trimmed).

Stored list values let any later item containing '/kg' trigger the match, so a drug whose primary dose is fixed but has a pediatric per-kg alternative would be miscounted. Reducing each list to its first population-plus-dose pair makes the LIKE test reflect the main single dose. The '<> ''' filter is unaffected because no stored value is empty.

drug.prescription_status.sql_expression: TRIM(CASE WHEN INSTR(prescription_status, '||') > 0 THEN SUBSTR(prescription_status, 1, INSTR(prescription_status, '||') - 1) ELSE prescription_status END)
drug.prescription_status.reason: The query tests whether a drug is 'prescription_only' to label it 'prescription only' versus 'other'. The one list value 'prescription_only||restricted' means the drug requires a prescription and also carries a restriction, so its first item 'prescription_only' is the status the author wants. Taking the first item of the list gives that result. Single-valued rows contain no separator and pass through unchanged, and TRIM handles any spaces around the separator.

disease.affected_organs.mapping_rule: For each distinct stored value, split on '||' into organ or tissue items. Replace each item with the body system(s) it belongs to, using the query's category names where they apply: 'nervous system', 'respiratory system', 'cardiovascular system', 'musculoskeletal system', 'urinary system'. Examples: 'lungs' -> 'respiratory system'; 'brain' -> 'nervous system'; 'heart' -> 'cardiovascular system'; 'joints||bones' -> 'musculoskeletal system'; 'kidney||bladder' -> 'urinary system'. Values with no item in the five systems map to 'other system' (or to the neutral label used for non-matching items). Keep '' as ''.

The LIKE patterns already handle '||' lists, so splitting is not the issue. The needed change is a knowledge mapping from organs to the body systems the query names.
